summary:
Mission Sky Is The Limit is a web tool that turns SPHEREx observations into short sky videos. You enter coordinates or click on an interactive Aladin map, set the size of the area, and the app fetches real SPHEREx cutouts from different dates, aligns them on the same grid and plays them in order. You can pause, step through frames, change the speed and see the date and quality flags for each image.

We built a searcher that finds moving objects automatically and checks them against Gaia and SkyBoT, so known asteroids are labelled and only new candidates are left. Stars can be shown over the map. The Infrared Explorer combines the 17 bands of each detector to get cleaner images, compares visits by blinking, summing or subtracting them, and shows the spectrum of any point you click. The view is saved in the URL, so it can be shared or embedded in other sites.

This matters because SPHEREx collects more data than scientists can check and catalogue by hand, and this project helps automate that process and connect regular people to this topic
details:
Mission: Sky is the Limit is a web app for spotting moving objects in NASA’s SPHEREx data. You pick a point on an interactive sky map, and the app fetches the SPHEREx images of that area taken on different dates. It lines them up and plays them like a short video, so anything that moves or changes brightness stands out.

You can search for an object by name or coordinates, or just click on the map, and then drag a circle to set the size of the search area. The app downloads real SPHEREx observations of that area from different dates and aligns them. We also built a detection tool that searches the area for moving objects by itself. It checks what it finds against Gaia and SkyBoT, so it can tell known asteroids apart from new candidates. The Infrared Explorer page uses all 102 wavelength bands from the six SPHEREx detectors, and you can click any point to see its spectrum.

SPHEREx collects far more images than scientists can check by hand. Volunteers comparing images have already found most of the comets and brown dwarfs we know of, and our app lets students and the public do the same search without writing any code. Every view can be shared with a link.

We built the backend in Python with Django, Astropy, astroquery, reproject and NumPy, and the frontend in JavaScript with Aladin for the sky map. The data comes from NASA’s IRSA archive, Gaia DR3, WISE, 2MASS and SkyBoT.

Most sky viewers only show images. Ours also searches for moving objects, names the ones that are already known, and uses the infrared spectrum that only SPHEREx provides.

We made sure new SPHEREx data releases are easy to add. When data is missing or a server is down, the app says clearly.
